analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal charter for companies offering small-dollar credit and check-cashing services to the unbanked.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 10 Democratic and 10 Republican cosponsors, it sat in a House Financial Services subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let companies that already serve people without bank accounts — payday lenders, check cashers, prepaid card issuers — obtain a new federal charter as Federal Financial Services and Credit Companies. The chartered companies would have had to offer disclosures, account access, and financial literacy programs, but short-term loans would have shown a fee 'per dollar' instead of the annual percentage rate used everywhere else, and federal charters would have overridden state laws that hit these companies differently. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then to its subcommittee on financial institutions, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The companies that would qualify for the charter — payday lenders, check-cashing stores, money transmitters, and prepaid card issuers — gain a federal charter, national standing, and protection from state laws that treat them differently. Unbanked and underbanked consumers gain guaranteed access to at least three financial products, standard disclosures, toll-free or online account access, and financial literacy help from any chartered company.

how_it_helps.text: Each chartered company must offer underbanked customers at least three financial products from a list including small-dollar credit, reloadable cards, check cashing, money orders, wire transfers, bill payment, and tax preparation.
Chartered companies must give clear cost disclosures, continuous account access by phone or internet, financial literacy materials, and help customers build their credit scores.

People with felony convictions within ten years are barred from owning or controlling a chartered company, and violations carry fines up to $20,000 per day or up to three years in prison, enforceable by state attorneys general when authorized.

The bill cites FDIC data that over 60 million low- and moderate-income Americans are unbanked, underbanked, or underserved, with unbanked rates far higher among Black (21.7%), Hispanic (19.3%), and low-income households.

analysis.who_pays: Low-income borrowers. Short-term loans would have disclosed the finance charge per dollar of credit rather than the annual percentage rate, which hides how expensive a two-week loan is on a yearly basis — the standard measure everywhere else in consumer credit. Federal charters would also have preempted any state law that applied to the chartered companies in a way the Comptroller deemed to have a discriminatory effect, overriding state payday-lending and consumer-protection rules.

drawbacks.text: For short-term credit, the bill replaces the annual percentage rate disclosure required under the Truth in Lending Act with a 'finance charge per dollar' statement, which makes a very expensive two-week loan look cheaper than it is on an annualized basis.

State law is preempted whenever applying it to a federally chartered company would have a 'discriminatory effect' on that company — a standard that could override state caps and restrictions on small-dollar lending.

Eligibility requires a demonstrated history of already serving underbanked customers, meaning the charter would flow to existing payday, check-cashing, and prepaid companies rather than new entrants, and the Comptroller of the Currency could approve any additional financial products the companies may offer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer-facing features — guaranteed product access, disclosures, literacy programs, and felony-background rules — are real, and millions of unbanked households genuinely lack affordable options. But the design tilts toward the industry: the per-dollar disclosure obscures annualized cost on exactly the short-term, high-fee products these companies sell, and federal preemption would strip away state consumer protections without substituting a rate cap or cost limit of any kind. A bill aimed at protecting underbanked borrowers would usually strengthen, not displace, the states that currently regulate this market.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2011, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, forwarded to its subcommittee on financial institutions that July, and never received a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Baca introduced the bill on May 13, 2011, with Reps. Meeks, Sires, and Schmidt as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.

On July 29, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where the record ends — no markup, no vote, and no further action through the end of the 112th Congress.
The bill attracted 20 cosponsors, split evenly between 10 Democrats and 10 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, state consumer-protection laws governing payday lending, check cashing, and small-dollar credit stayed in force, and the alternative financial services industry never received the federal charter and preemption it would have gained. Borrowers who rely on state rate caps and disclosure rules are no worse off than before.

for.name: Rep. Joe Baca
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a markup or reported it out; it was forwarded to a subcommittee and stayed there.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was evenly split — 10 Democrats and 10 Republicans — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Payday lenders and short-term consumer credit companies
industries.note: The bill would have given these companies a permanent federal charter, a dedicated regulator, and preemption of state laws that restrict them. Its disclosure rule for short-term loans states the fee per dollar instead of the annual percentage rate, which downplays how costly these loans are over a year — and the companies profit from exactly those fees charged to low-income borrowers.

industries.industry: Check cashing, money transfer, and prepaid card companies
industries.note: These firms would have qualified for the charter and gained federal standing for fee-based services like check cashing, wire transfers, and reloadable cards. The same charter would have required them to add disclosures, account access, and financial literacy programs.

industries.industry: State consumer-protection regulators and attorneys general
industries.note: Federal charters would have preempted state laws that apply differently to the chartered companies, weakening state rate caps and lending rules. States would have kept only the enforcement powers the Comptroller chose to authorize.
